chapters.t: The reader and his two transmitters
p: The reader: Ibn Kathīr is Abū Maʿbad ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kathīr ibn ʿUmar al-Makkī, born in Makkah in 45 AH and died in 120 AH. He was one of the Successors, met Companions such as Anas ibn Mālik and Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī, and learned the Qurʾān from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Sāʾib, Mujāhid ibn Jabr and Dirbās the freedman of Ibn ʿAbbās. His was the reading of the people of Makkah, and Imām al-Shāfiʿī recited by it.
Al-Bazzī: Abū al-Ḥasan Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Qāsim ibn Nāfiʿ ibn Abī Bazzah al-Makkī (170–250 AH), the muʾadhdhin of al-Masjid al-Ḥarām and the leading reciter of Makkah in his time.
Qunbul: Abū ʿAmr Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Khālid al-Makkī (195–291 AH), the leading reciter of the Ḥijāz and one of the teachers of Abū Bakr ibn Mujāhid.
Chain: Neither transmitter read to Ibn Kathīr himself; both received his reading through his students.
Way: The rules below follow the way of the Shāṭibiyyah (Ḥirz al-Amānī wa-Wajh al-Tahānī, the poem of Imām al-Shāṭibī on the seven readings) and are described by comparison with the riwāyah of Ḥafṣ.
Between two sūrahs: Ibn Kathīr joins the end of one sūrah to the beginning of the next in one way only, with the basmalah between them.

Al-Anfāl and al-Tawbah: The exception is the passage from al-Anfāl to al-Tawbah, which has no basmalah. Here, as for all readers, the two sūrahs are either joined directly (waṣl) or separated by a short pause without breath (sakt).
Al-Fātiḥah: Ibn Kathīr counts the basmalah as the first āyah of al-Fātiḥah.
Mālik: He reads مَلِكِ يَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ without an alif after the mīm, where Ḥafṣ reads مَٰلِكِ.

Ṣirāṭ: Qunbul reads this word with sīn wherever it occurs in the Qurʾān, with or without the definite article: ٱهْدِنَا ٱلسِّرَٰطَ ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمَ and سِرَٰطَ ٱلَّذِينَ. Al-Bazzī reads it with ṣād like Ḥafṣ.
Madd muttaṣil: When the hamzah follows the madd letter inside the same word, the madd is lengthened to four ḥarakāt, as in جَآءَ, سُوٓءٍ and سَوَآءٌ.

Madd munfaṣil: When the madd letter ends one word and the hamzah begins the next, Ibn Kathīr reads with qaṣr only, two ḥarakāt, where Ḥafṣ lengthens. Examples: فِي أُمِّهَا, قَالُوا إِنَّا, يَٰأَيُّهَا. The ṣilah before a hamzah is treated the same way: وَأَمْرُهُۥ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ.
Madd ʿāriḍ: When a madd is followed by a sukūn that arises only because of stopping, all readers allow two, four or six ḥarakāt.

Madd before an altered hamzah: When a madd letter comes before a hamzah that has been eased, replaced or dropped, both lengthening and shortening are allowed. Lengthening is preferred when a trace of the hamzah remains (tashīl), and shortening when nothing of it remains.

Before a vowelled letter: In connected recitation Ibn Kathīr gives the plural mīm a ḍammah and joins it to a wāw of two ḥarakāt (ṣilah) whenever the next letter is vowelled, whether that letter is a hamzah or not. Ḥafṣ reads the mīm with sukūn. Examples: عَلَيْهِمُۥ غَيْرِ ٱلْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمُۥ وَلَا ٱلضَّآلِّينَ (1:7) and وَٱجْتَبَيْنَٰهُمُۥ وَهَدَيْنَٰهُمُۥ إِلَىٰ صِرَٰطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ (6:87).

Before a sākin letter: The mīm takes a ḍammah without ṣilah, as for all readers, because the wāw would meet the following sākin: مِنْهُمُ ٱلْمُؤْمِنُونَ (3:110), عَلَيْهِمُ ٱلْقِتَالُ, بِهِمُ ٱلْأَسْبَابُ.
In waqf: The ṣilah belongs to waṣl only; when stopping on the mīm it is sākinah.
Between two vowelled letters: The pronoun hāʾ is joined to a wāw or yāʾ of two ḥarakāt by all readers: مَالُهُۥ إِذَا (92:11), رَبِّهِۦ فَصَلَّىٰ (87:15).

After a sākin letter: Ibn Kathīr alone also makes ṣilah when the hāʾ is preceded by a sākin and followed by a vowelled letter: مِنْهُۥ, عَلَيْهِۦ, فِيهِۦ, فَٱتَّبِعُوهُۥ. Ḥafṣ does this only in فِيهِۦ مُهَانًا (25:69).
Before a sākin letter: There is no ṣilah. In عَلَيْهِ ٱللَّهَ (48:10) Ibn Kathīr reads the hāʾ with kasrah, where Ḥafṣ reads it with ḍammah.
Arjiʾhu: In 7:111 and 26:36 he reads أَرْجِئْهُۥ وَأَخَاهُ with a sākin hamzah after the jīm and the hāʾ with ḍammah and ṣilah. Ḥafṣ reads أَرْجِهْ.
Wa-yattaqihi: In 24:52 he reads وَيَتَّقِهِۦ with kasrah on the qāf and the hāʾ with kasrah and ṣilah. Ḥafṣ alone reads the qāf with sukūn.
Ansānīhi: In 18:63 he reads وَمَآ أَنسَىٰنِيهِۦ إِلَّا with kasrah and ṣilah. Ḥafṣ reads the hāʾ with ḍammah.
Fa-alqihi: In 27:28 he reads فَأَلْقِهِۦ إِلَيْهِمْ with kasrah and ṣilah. Ḥafṣ reads the hāʾ with sukūn.
Yarḍahu: In 39:7 he reads يَرْضَهُۥ لَكُمْ with ḍammah and ṣilah.
Elsewhere: The remaining words of this chapter are read with ṣilah as Ḥafṣ reads them.

General rule: When an interrogative hamzah (always with fatḥah) is followed by another hamzah in the same word, Ibn Kathīr pronounces the first fully and the second with tashīl, that is, between a hamzah and the madd letter matching its vowel, whether that vowel is fatḥah, kasrah or ḍammah. Ḥafṣ pronounces both fully. Examples: ءَأَنذَرْتَهُمْ (2:6), أَءِذَا, أَءُنزِلَ (38:8).

Added interrogative hamzah: In some words Ibn Kathīr reads an interrogative hamzah followed by an eased hamzah where Ḥafṣ has a single hamzah: ءَأَذْهَبْتُمْ (46:20), أَءِنَّكُمْ لَتَأْتُونَ (7:81) and ءَأَن يُؤْتَىٰ أَحَدٌ (3:73).

Āmantum: In 7:123, 20:71 and 26:49 al-Bazzī reads ءَامَنتُمْ with an interrogative hamzah, then an eased hamzah, then the alif. Qunbul reads so in al-Shuʿarāʾ. In Ṭāhā he reads with one hamzah like Ḥafṣ. In al-Aʿrāf, when joining to the preceding word, he turns the first hamzah into a wāw: قَالَ فِرْعَوْنُ وَءَامَنتُمْ; when beginning from the word he reads the hamzah.
A-amintum in al-Mulk: Qunbul likewise turns the first hamzah into a wāw in waṣl only in ٱلنُّشُورُ وَأَمِنتُمْ (67:15–16), the second hamzah remaining eased.
A single hamzah in Yūsuf: In 12:90 Ibn Kathīr reads إِنَّكَ لَأَنتَ يُوسُفُ with one hamzah, as a statement, where Ḥafṣ reads أَءِنَّكَ.

Repeated question: In the eleven places where a question is repeated within one passage, such as أَءِذَا كُنَّا تُرَٰبًا أَءِنَّا لَفِي خَلْقٍ جَدِيدٍ (13:5), Ibn Kathīr reads question and statement exactly where Ḥafṣ does; the only difference is that he eases the second hamzah of each question.

Scope: These rules apply only when a word ending in a hamzah is joined to a word beginning with one; if the reciter stops on the first word, both hamzahs are pronounced fully. Ḥafṣ pronounces both fully in every case.
Different vowels, first with fatḥah: Both transmitters ease the second hamzah: تَفِيٓءَ إِلَىٰ (49:9), جَآءَ أُمَّةً (23:44).

Different vowels, second with fatḥah: Both transmitters replace the second hamzah with a pure letter carrying fatḥah: a wāw after ḍammah, as in نَشَآءُ أَصَبْنَٰهُم (7:100) and ٱلسُّفَهَآءُ أَلَآ (2:13), and a yāʾ after kasrah, as in مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ ءَايَةً (26:4) and ٱلنِّسَآءِ أَوْ (2:235).

Ḍammah then kasrah: The second hamzah is read in two ways, with tashīl or replaced by a wāw with kasrah: يَشَآءُ إِلَىٰ (2:142), ٱلشُّهَدَآءُ إِذَا (2:282), ٱلْفُقَرَآءُ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ (35:15). The source gives tashīl as the preferred way for Qunbul and ibdāl as the preferred way for al-Bazzī.
Same vowels: Here the transmitters differ. Al-Bazzī alters the first hamzah and Qunbul alters the second.

Al-Bazzī, two fatḥahs: He drops the first hamzah, so جَآءَ أَمْرُنَا (11:40) is read جَا أَمْرُنَا and جَآءَ أَحَدٌ is read جَا أَحَدٌ. The alif before the dropped hamzah may be read with two ḥarakāt, which is preferred, or with four.

Al-Bazzī, two kasrahs or two ḍammahs: He eases the first hamzah, and the madd before it may be read with four or two ḥarakāt: هَٰؤُلَآءِ إِن (2:31), مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ إِن (34:9), أَوْلِيَآءُ أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ (46:32), the only case of two ḍammahs.
Al-Bazzī in bi-l-sūʾi illā: In 12:53 he has a second way besides tashīl: the first hamzah becomes a wāw and the wāw before it is merged into it, giving بِٱلسُّوِّ إِلَّا with a doubled wāw.

Qunbul, same vowels: He reads the second hamzah in two ways, with tashīl or replaced by a madd letter (ibdāl). In ibdāl the madd is six ḥarakāt when a sākin letter follows, as in جَآءَ أَمْرُنَا, شَآءَ أَنشَرَهُۥ (80:22), مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ إِن and أَهَٰؤُلَآءِ إِيَّاكُمْ (34:40), and two ḥarakāt when a vowelled letter follows, as in أَوْلِيَآءُ أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ.

Qunbul, ibdāl with two lengths: When the following sākin takes a temporary vowel, as in ٱلنِّسَآءِ إِنِ ٱتَّقَيْتُنَّ (33:32), or when an alif follows, as in جَآءَ ءَالَ لُوطٍ (15:61) and جَآءَ ءَالَ فِرْعَوْنَ (54:41), the madd is read with two or six ḥarakāt.
Ibdāl: Ibn Kathīr replaces the sākin hamzah with an alif in يَاجُوجَ وَمَاجُوجَ (18:94, 21:96) and with a wāw in مُوصَدَةٌ (90:20, 104:8). Ḥafṣ reads both with hamzah.
Yuḍāhūna: In 9:30 he reads يُضَٰهُونَ without a hamzah, where Ḥafṣ reads يُضَٰهِـُٔونَ.

Allāʾī: Ibn Kathīr reads this word (33:4, 58:2, 65:4) without the yāʾ after the hamzah. Qunbul reads ٱلَّٰٓءِ with a full hamzah in waṣl and waqf. Al-Bazzī has two ways. The first is tashīl of the hamzah, with the alif before it read four or two ḥarakāt, stopping with tashīl and rawm. The second is replacing the hamzah with a sākin yāʾ, ٱلَّٰٓيْ, with a madd of six ḥarakāt, in waṣl and waqf.
Allāʾī before yaʾisna: In وَٱلَّٰٓيْ يَئِسْنَ (65:4), by the second way, al-Bazzī reads the sākin yāʾ before the next yāʾ either with iẓhār and a brief sakt, which is preferred, or with idghām.
Hā-antum: Al-Bazzī reads هَٰأَنتُمْ with an alif after the hāʾ, as a madd munfaṣil of two ḥarakāt, and a full hamzah. Qunbul reads هَأَنتُمْ without the alif.
Added hamzah with madd: Ibn Kathīr reads زَكَرِيَّآءُ, مِيكَآئِيلَ (2:98) and وَمَنَوٰٓءَةَ (53:20) with a hamzah and a madd muttaṣil, where Ḥafṣ has no hamzah.

Other added hamzahs: He reads تُرْجِئُ (33:51) and مُرْجَـُٔونَ (9:106) with a hamzah carrying ḍammah, ضِئْزَىٰ (53:22) with a sākin hamzah, and كُفُؤًا (112:4) and هُزُؤًا with a hamzah where Ḥafṣ reads a wāw.

Qunbul in sūq: In بِٱلسُّؤْقِ (38:33) and عَلَىٰ سُؤْقِهِۦ (48:29) Qunbul alone adds a hamzah, either a sākin hamzah in place of the wāw, which is preferred, or a hamzah with ḍammah followed by the wāw: بِٱلسُّؤُوقِ, سُؤُوقِهِۦ.
Qunbul in ḍiyāʾ: In 10:5, 21:48 and 28:71 Qunbul reads ضِئَآءً with a hamzah in place of the yāʾ.

Al-Bazzī in yayʾas: In the five verbs of this root in Yūsuf and al-Raʿd (12:80, 12:87 twice, 12:110, 13:31) al-Bazzī has two ways. One is like Ḥafṣ. The other, preferred, moves the hamzah before the yāʾ and turns it into an alif, leaving the yāʾ with fatḥah: ٱسْتَايَسُوا, وَلَا تَايَسُوا, لَا يَايَسُ, ٱسْتَايَسَ, أَفَلَمْ يَايَسِ.

Al-Bazzī, keeping one way: The source notes that whoever reads the second way of yayʾas for al-Bazzī should read لَأَعْنَتَكُمْ (2:220) with tashīl of the hamzah and وَلِي دِينِ (109:6) with a sākin yāʾ, so that the ways of transmission are not mixed.
Wa-lā adrākum: In 10:16 al-Bazzī has two ways: وَلَآ أَدْرَىٰكُم with the alif like Ḥafṣ, and وَلَأَدْرَىٰكُم without the alif, which is preferred.
Al-Qurʾān: Ibn Kathīr moves the fatḥah of the hamzah onto the sākin rāʾ and drops the hamzah in this word throughout the Qurʾān, with or without the definite article: ٱلْقُرَانُ, قُرَانًا.
Laykah: In 26:176 and 38:13 he reads أَصْحَٰبُ لَيْكَةَ, with a lām carrying fatḥah, no hamzah, and fatḥah on the tāʾ. Ḥafṣ reads لْـَٔيْكَةِ.

The imperative of saʾala: When this imperative follows a wāw or a fāʾ, he moves the vowel of the hamzah onto the sīn and drops the hamzah: وَسَلِ ٱلْقَرْيَةَ (12:82), فَسَلُوا أَهْلَ ٱلذِّكْرِ (16:43), وَسَلُوا مَآ أَنفَقْتُمْ (60:10).
Dhāl before tāʾ: Ibn Kathīr reads أَخَذْتُمْ, ٱتَّخَذْتُمْ, أَخَذْتَ, ٱتَّخَذْتَ and similar forms with iẓhār of the dhāl, like Ḥafṣ.
Irkab maʿanā: In 11:42 al-Bazzī has two ways: idghām of the bāʾ into the mīm like Ḥafṣ, ٱرْكَب مَّعَنَا, and iẓhār, ٱرْكَبْ مَعَنَا, which the source prefers.
Yalhath dhālika: In 7:176 Ibn Kathīr reads يَلْهَثْ ذَٰلِكَ with iẓhār of the thāʾ, where Ḥafṣ merges it.
Yuʿadhdhib man: In 2:284 Ibn Kathīr reads both verbs with sukūn, فَيَغْفِرْ لِمَن يَشَآءُ وَيُعَذِّبْ مَن يَشَآءُ, with iẓhār of the bāʾ before the mīm. Ḥafṣ reads both verbs with ḍammah.

No imālah: Ibn Kathīr reads everything with fatḥ and has no imālah anywhere, not even in the one word Ḥafṣ reads with imālah (11:41), which Ibn Kathīr reads مُجْرَىٰهَا with ḍammah on the mīm and a plain fatḥah.

No sakt: The pauses of Ḥafṣ belong to Ḥafṣ alone. Ibn Kathīr joins عِوَجًا قَيِّمًا (18:1–2) and مَرْقَدِنَا هَٰذَا (36:52) without pausing, and reads مَن رَّاقٍ (75:27) and بَل رَّانَ (83:14) with idghām.

Feminine tāʾ written open: Ibn Kathīr stops with a hāʾ on feminine nouns that the muṣḥaf writes with an open tāʾ, where Ḥafṣ stops with a tāʾ. Among them are رَحْمَتَ, نِعْمَتَ, سُنَّتَ, لَعْنَتَ, ٱمْرَأَتَ, مَعْصِيَتِ, قُرَّتُ, شَجَرَتَ, جَنَّتُ, ٱبْنَتَ, فِطْرَتَ, بَقِيَّتُ and كَلِمَتُ.
Yā abati: He stops on يَٰأَبَتِ with a sākin hāʾ: يَٰأَبَهْ.
Hayhāta: Al-Bazzī stops on هَيْهَاتَ (23:36) with a hāʾ.

Interrogative mā: On the five words made of a preposition and the interrogative mā, al-Bazzī stops in two ways, on a sākin mīm or with hāʾ al-sakt: فِيمَهْ, مِمَّهْ, عَمَّهْ, لِمَهْ, بِمَهْ. Examples: عَمَّ يَتَسَآءَلُونَ (78:1), فِيمَ أَنتَ (79:43), مِمَّ خُلِقَ (86:5), لِمَ تَقُولُونَ (61:2), بِمَ يَرْجِعُ (27:35).
Rule: In thirty-one places al-Bazzī doubles the tāʾ at the beginning of a present-tense verb when joining it to what precedes. Qunbul reads a single tāʾ like Ḥafṣ.
After a madd letter: The madd before the doubled tāʾ is lengthened to six ḥarakāt: وَلَا تَّيَمَّمُوا (2:267), وَلَا تَّفَرَّقُوا (3:103), وَلَا تَّعَاوَنُوا (5:2), لَا تَّنَاصَرُونَ (37:25).
After other letters: فَتَّفَرَّقَ بِكُمْ (6:153), ٱلَّذِينَ تَّوَفَّىٰهُمُ (4:97), فَإِن تَّوَلَّوْا (11:57), إِذْ تَّلَقَّوْنَهُۥ (24:15), نَارًا تَّلَظَّىٰ (92:14).

Further places named: لَا تَّكَلَّمُ (11:105), وَلَا تَّبَرَّجْنَ (33:33), أَن تَّبَدَّلَ (33:52), وَلَا تَّنَابَزُوا (49:11), وَلَا تَّجَسَّسُوا (49:12), لِتَّعَارَفُوٓا (49:13), أَن تَّوَلَّوْهُمْ (60:9), لَمَا تَّخَيَّرُونَ (68:38), and the verbs تَّنَزَّلُ and تَّلَقَّفُ.
Where: Al-Bazzī transmitted saying the takbīr at the end of each sūrah from al-Ḍuḥā to al-Nās.
Wording: The preferred form is Allāhu akbar.
How: When the end of a sūrah is joined to the takbīr, the usual rule for the meeting of the two is applied; then the basmalah is read, then the beginning of the next sūrah.
Status: The takbīr is not part of the Qurʾān and is not written in the muṣḥaf. It is a remembrance like the istiʿādhah, and a sunnah.

Definition: The yāʾ of the first person attached to a noun, verb or particle is written in the muṣḥaf, and the readers differ over reading it with fatḥah or sukūn in 212 places, grouped by the letter that follows.

Before a hamzah with fatḥah (99 places): Ibn Kathīr generally reads the yāʾ with fatḥah, as in إِنِّيَ أَعْلَمُ and إِنِّيَ أَخَافُ, and also in ذَرُونِيَ أَقْتُلْ (40:26), ٱدْعُونِيَ أَسْتَجِبْ (40:60) and فَٱذْكُرُونِيَ أَذْكُرْكُمْ (2:152). Ḥafṣ reads these with sukūn.

Before a hamzah with fatḥah, transmitters differ: Al-Bazzī reads with fatḥah and Qunbul with sukūn in أَوْزِعْنِيَ أَنْ (27:19, 46:15), وَلَٰكِنِّيَ أَرَىٰكُمْ (11:29, 46:23), إِنِّيَ أَرَىٰكُم (11:84), فَطَرَنِيَ أَفَلَا (11:51) and مِن تَحْتِيَ أَفَلَا (43:51). In عِندِي أَوَلَمْ (28:78) it is the reverse: al-Bazzī reads sukūn and Qunbul fatḥah.
Before a hamzah with fatḥah, sukūn: Like all readers he reads sukūn in أَرْنِي أَنظُرْ (7:143), وَلَا تَفْتِنِّي أَلَا (9:49), وَتَرْحَمْنِي أَكُن (11:47) and فَٱتَّبِعْنِي أَهْدِكَ (19:43).
Before a hamzah with kasrah (52 places): He reads sukūn, except two with fatḥah: ءَابَآءِيَ إِبْرَٰهِيمَ (12:38) and دُعَآءِيَ إِلَّا (71:6).
Before a hamzah with ḍammah (10 places): He reads all of them with sukūn.
Before the definite article (14 places): He reads with fatḥah, as in عَهْدِيَ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ (2:124), which Ḥafṣ reads with sukūn.

Before another hamzat al-waṣl (7 places): Ibn Kathīr reads with fatḥah in إِنِّيَ ٱصْطَفَيْتُكَ (7:144), أَخِيَ ٱشْدُدْ (20:30–31), لِنَفْسِيَ ٱذْهَبْ (20:41–42), ذِكْرِيَ ٱذْهَبَا (20:42–43) and بَعْدِيَ ٱسْمُهُۥ (61:6). In قَوْمِيَ ٱتَّخَذُوا (25:30) al-Bazzī reads fatḥah and Qunbul sukūn.

Before any other letter (30 places): Ibn Kathīr reads with fatḥah in شُرَكَآءِيَ قَالُوا (41:47) and مِن وَرَآءِيَ وَكَانَتِ (19:5). In وَلِي دِينِ (109:6) al-Bazzī has two ways, sukūn, which is preferred, and fatḥah; Qunbul reads sukūn.

Where Ḥafṣ reads fatḥah: The source then lists بَيْتِي (2:125, 22:26, 71:28), وَجْهِي (3:20, 6:79), لِي (14:22, 20:18, 38:23, 38:69) and مَعِي (7:105, 9:83, 18:67, 18:72, 18:75, 21:24, 26:62, 26:118, 28:34). Ḥafṣ reads these with fatḥah and Ibn Kathīr with sukūn.
Definition: These are yāʾs at the end of words that are left out of the muṣḥaf's writing; the readers differ over pronouncing them. They are 62 in all.

In waṣl and waqf: Ibn Kathīr pronounces the yāʾ both when joining and when stopping in twenty words: يَأْتِي (11:105), تُؤْتُونِي (12:66), ٱلْمُتَعَالِي (13:9), أَخَّرْتَنِي (17:62), يَهْدِيَنِي (18:24), تَرَنِي (18:39), يُؤْتِيَنِي (18:40), نَبْغِي (18:64), تُعَلِّمَنِي (18:66), تَتَّبِعَنِي (20:93), وَٱلْبَادِي (22:25), أَتُمِدُّونَنِي (27:36), كَٱلْجَوَابِي (34:13), ٱلتَّلَاقِي (40:15), ٱلتَّنَادِي (40:32), ٱتَّبِعُونِي أَهْدِكُمْ (40:38), ٱلْجَوَارِي (42:32), ٱلْمُنَادِي (50:41), إِلَى ٱلدَّاعِي (54:8) and يَسْرِي (89:4). Ḥafṣ omits the yāʾ in all of them.
Bi-l-wādī: In 89:9 Ibn Kathīr reads بِٱلْوَادِي with the yāʾ; in waqf Qunbul has two ways, with and without it.
Al-Bazzī alone: He pronounces the yāʾ in دُعَآءِي (14:40), يَدْعُ ٱلدَّاعِي (54:6), أَكْرَمَنِي (89:15) and أَهَٰنَنِي (89:16).
Qunbul alone: He pronounces the yāʾ in مَن يَتَّقِي وَيَصْبِرْ (12:90).
In waqf only: Ibn Kathīr stops with a yāʾ on بَاقٍ (16:96) and on هَادٍ, وَالٍ and وَاقٍ wherever they occur: بَاقِي, هَادِي, وَالِي, وَاقِي.
The yāʾ Ḥafṣ keeps: In فَمَآ ءَاتَىٰنِ ٱللَّهُ (27:36), the one place where Ḥafṣ pronounces an extra yāʾ, Ibn Kathīr omits it.

The first of two sākins: When a sākin at the end of a word meets a verb that begins with hamzat al-waṣl and whose third letter carries a permanent ḍammah, Ibn Kathīr gives the first sākin a ḍammah, where Ḥafṣ gives it a kasrah: قُلُ ٱدْعُوا ٱللَّهَ أَوُ ٱدْعُوا ٱلرَّحْمَٰنَ (17:110), وَقَالَتُ ٱخْرُجْ (12:31), وَلَقَدُ ٱسْتُهْزِئَ (6:10). The tanwīn is treated the same way in مَحْظُورًا ٱنظُرْ (17:20–21).
Khuṭuwāt: Al-Bazzī reads خُطْوَٰتِ with a sākin ṭāʾ wherever it occurs; Qunbul reads خُطُوَٰتِ with ḍammah like Ḥafṣ.
Words read with sukūn: Ibn Kathīr reads a sākin middle letter in أُكْلَهَا, ٱلْأُكْلِ and أُكْلٍ, in ٱلْقُدْسِ, in أَرْنَا and أَرْنِي, and a light sākin yāʾ in ٱلْمَيْتِ and مَيْتٍ.

Words read with kasrah: He reads the present tense of ḥasiba with kasrah on the sīn, as in تَحْسِبُ, يَحْسِبُونَ and يَحْسِبُهُمُ, and a kasrah on the first letter of بِيُوتٍ, ٱلْبِيُوتَ, عِيُونٍ and شِيُوخًا.
Words read with ḍammah: He reads جُثِيًّا, عُتِيًّا and صُلِيًّا with ḍammah on the first letter, and مُتُّ, مُتَّ and مُتُّمْ with ḍammah on the mīm.
Mubayyinah: He reads مُبَيَّنَةٍ and مُبَيَّنَٰتٍ with fatḥah on the yāʾ.
Words with madd muttaṣil: He reads وَكَآئِن where Ḥafṣ reads وَكَأَيِّن, and ٱلنَّشَآءَةَ where Ḥafṣ reads ٱلنَّشْأَةَ.
Four further words: The source also lists نِسْيًا (19:23), تَسَّٰقَطْ (19:25), مُخْلِصًا (19:51) and تَلَقَّفُ, which Ḥafṣ reads نَسْيًا, تُسَٰقِطْ, مُخْلَصًا and تَلْقَفُ.

The nūn of the dual: Ibn Kathīr doubles the nūn of dual relative and demonstrative pronouns. In وَٱلَّذَآنِّ (4:16) and هَٰذَآنِّ (20:63, 22:19) the alif before it is lengthened to six ḥarakāt. In هَٰتَيْنِّ (28:27) and ٱلَّذَيْنِّ (41:29) the yāʾ may be read with six, four or two ḥarakāt.
